{"id":"PKIX-rgc6","title":"SMTP-DANE (RFC 7672): dedicated entry point, not a reuse of the HTTPS DANE path","description":"## Why

RFC 7672 SMTP-DANE has the strongest production deployment of any DANE flavour — MTAs negotiating TLS routinely use it for trust. A workspace that adopts DANE for HTTPS and not SMTP is incomplete. Replaces PKIX-j32w.6, which asked the question against a function (verify_smtp_signer) that does not exist and would have been the wrong home anyway: SMTP-DANE validates a mail SERVER's TLS certificate, not a signer.

## Why this cannot reuse verify_tls_server's DANE path

Three behavioural differences from HTTPS-DANE. The first makes a shared path wrong rather than merely incomplete.

### 1. Usage filtering — CONFIRM THIS FIRST

Current understanding is that RFC 7672 requires SMTP clients to ignore PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1) records outright, because public CA trust is not meaningful between MTAs with no user to see a warning: only DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) apply.

THIS IS NOT CONFIRMED. Read RFC 7672 §3.1 and the surrounding text before writing any code. If it holds, then a shared code path with verify_tls_server would honour usage-0 and usage-1 records that SMTP-DANE requires be ignored — a silent policy violation, and the reason this needs its own entry point. If it does not hold, re-evaluate whether a shared path with a mode flag is adequate after all.

### 2. DNSSEC-validated MX lookup — reaches into the resolver

The TLSA owner name derives from an MX lookup, and that lookup must itself be DNSSEC-validated. An unvalidated MX lookup lets an attacker rewrite the MX record and point the connection at a server whose TLSA record they also control, which defeats the whole mechanism.

This is a pkix-dane-resolver requirement, not a wrapper concern: it needs a validated multi-step lookup (MX, then TLSA under the resulting hostname), with the DNSSEC status of BOTH steps surfaced. pkix-dane's TlsaResolver trait as shipped resolves a single TlsaName and has no MX concept. Expect either an additional trait method or a sibling trait in pkix-dane-resolver. Check whether this changes what PKIX-j32w.2 should build before that bead starts.

### 3. Reference identity

Which name the certificate must match follows RFC 7672's MX-derived rules rather than RFC 6125 hostname matching. Determine how this composes with pkix-identity rather than reimplementing name matching.

## Placement — open

PKIX-j32w.6 left this open: pkix-chain wrapper, or a sibling pkix-smtp crate. Decide once the resolver-side shape from difference 2 is known, since an MX-aware resolver trait may make a sibling crate the natural home.

## Also in scope

- RFC 7672's own opportunistic-vs-mandatory posture at the SMTP level, and how it composes with the DaneFailurePolicy decided in PKIX-j32w.4. These are different layers and may not agree; work out which wins.
- Whether the dane / dane-resolver feature split decided on PKIX-j32w.3 extends here unchanged.

## Depends on

pkix-dane 0.2.0 (shipped). Resolver work is PKIX-j32w.2; this bead should be read before that one starts, because difference 2 may widen its scope.

## Acceptance

[ ] RFC 7672 usage-filtering requirement confirmed against the RFC text and recorded
[ ] MX lookup is DNSSEC-validated, with the status of both lookup steps surfaced to the caller
[ ] Usage 0 and 1 records handled per the confirmed RFC requirement
[ ] Reference identity follows RFC 7672, composed with pkix-identity rather than reimplemented
[ ] Placement decided and recorded","status":"open","priority":3,"issue_type":"feature","owner":"mark@reviewcommit.com","created_at":"2026-11-24T19:25:04.79877682Z","created_by":"Mark Atwood","updated_at":"2026-11-24T19:25:04.79877682Z"}

{"notes":"RESEARCH DONE 2026-11-24, against the RFC text. THIS BEAD'S CENTRAL PREMISE WAS WRONG and is corrected below. No code written: the bead said to confirm first, and confirming changed the design.

## CORRECTION: usage 0/1 is NOT a MUST-ignore

This bead stated, flagged as unconfirmed, that "RFC 7672 requires SMTP clients to ignore PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1) records outright" and that a shared code path with verify_tls_server would therefore be "a silent policy violation". That is not what the RFC says.

RFC 7672 section 3.1.3, verbatim:

  "Therefore, TLSA records for the port 25 SMTP service used by client MTAs
   SHOULD NOT include TLSA RRs with certificate usage PKIX-TA(0) or
   PKIX-EE(1)."

  "SMTP client treatment of TLSA RRs with certificate usages PKIX-TA(0) or
   PKIX-EE(1) is undefined.  As with any other unsupported certificate
   usage, SMTP clients MAY treat such records as 'unusable'."

So: SHOULD NOT PUBLISH on the server side, and UNDEFINED with a MAY on the client side. Honouring usage 0/1 in an SMTP client would be implementing undefined behaviour, which is permitted. It is still the wrong thing to do -- the RFC's reasoning is that PKIX usages cannot aid SMTP TLS security because an attacker who can compromise DNSSEC can simply substitute a non-PKIX usage, and MTAs have no agreed CA list and no user to click OK -- but we would be following a MAY, not complying with a MUST. The implementation should say so rather than claiming compliance it does not have.

Consequence: usage filtering NO LONGER CARRIES the separate-entry-point argument. That argument now rests entirely on the two other differences, both of which survive.

## What the RFC actually requires, confirmed

1. DANE-EE(3) name checks, section 3.2.1: "The SMTP client MUST NOT perform certificate name checks". pkix-dane's verify_dane_ee ALREADY does no name check, per RFC 7671 section 5.1. Nothing to do.

2. DANE-TA(2) name checks, section 3.2.2: the client MUST perform name checks, and MUST use the TLSA BASE DOMAIN as the primary reference identifier. Additionally:
   - if the base domain came from a "secure" MX lookup, the original next-hop domain MUST be a second reference identifier
   - the CNAME-expanded original next-hop domain MUST be a third, if different
   - when using DANE despite "insecure" MX redirection, the MX hostname is the ONLY reference identifier
   So this is a SET of reference identifiers derived from the lookup chain, not one hostname. That shape is genuinely different from verify_tls_server's single ServerName.

3. Reference identifier matching, section 3.2.3: only DNS-IDs are matched if any are present; THE CN-ID IS CONSIDERED WHEN NO DNS-IDs ARE PRESENT. Wildcards valid in either, must be the entire first label, and MUST match exactly one label by default.

4. Section 3.2: "When at least one usable 'secure' TLSA record is found, the SMTP client MUST use TLSA records to authenticate the SMTP server. Messages MUST NOT be delivered via the SMTP server if authentication fails." So RFC 7672 is opportunistic about WHETHER DANE is available and MANDATORY once a usable secure record exists. That is a sharper posture than DaneFailurePolicy::Opportunistic and needs reconciling with it, not merely composing.

## NEW BLOCKER FOUND: pkix-identity cannot be reused as-is

RFC 7672 section 3.2.3 requires CN-ID fallback when no DNS-IDs are present. pkix-identity deliberately refuses it. Its rustdoc:

  "Does not consult the certificate's Subject DN CN attribute -- CN fallback
   was deprecated by RFC 6125 section 6.4.4 and is intentionally not
   performed. A certificate that carries identity only in its CN is rejected
   with IdentityError::MissingSan."

Both positions are correct for their context: RFC 6125 deprecated CN fallback for web PKI, and RFC 7672 kept it for MTA-to-MTA where certificates are often ancient and self-managed. But it means SMTP-DANE name checks cannot simply call pkix_identity::verify_dns_name.

Decide before implementing: an opt-in CN-ID mode on pkix-identity, or an SMTP-specific matcher. Leaning toward an opt-in on pkix-identity, since the wildcard and case-folding logic is there and worth reusing, and a second matcher invites the two to diverge -- but it means putting a deprecated-for-web behaviour behind a flag in a crate that currently refuses it on principle, which deserves a deliberate decision.

## Revised scope

Three pieces, in dependency order:

A. Reference-identifier matching for SMTP: the identifier SET from section 3.2.2 plus the matching rules from section 3.2.3, including the CN-ID question above. Pure, testable, no I/O. Smallest piece and the one that unblocks the rest.

B. DNSSEC-validated MX lookup in pkix-dane-resolver: a validated two-step lookup (MX, then TLSA under the resulting hostname) with the DNSSEC status of BOTH steps surfaced, since section 3.2.2's identifier set depends on whether the MX lookup was secure. pkix-dane's TlsaResolver resolves a single TlsaName and has no MX concept. Also needs sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 (MX resolution, non-MX destinations) and 2.1.1 (bogus/indeterminate handling), none of which I have read yet.

C. The entry point itself, and its placement. Still open between a pkix-chain wrapper and a sibling crate; B's shape should decide it.

## Not yet read

Sections 2.1.1 to 2.1.3 (DNS errors, bogus and indeterminate responses, stub resolver considerations), 2.2.1 to 2.2.3 (MX resolution, non-MX destinations, TLSA record lookup), and section 8.1 (SNI support). Piece B should not be designed without them; section 2.1.1 in particular will bear on how DaneFailurePolicy composes.

## Acceptance, revised

[x] RFC 7672 usage-filtering requirement confirmed against the RFC text and recorded -- it is undefined/MAY, not MUST, and this bead's original claim was wrong
[ ] Decide CN-ID: opt-in on pkix-identity, or an SMTP-specific matcher
[ ] Reconcile section 3.2's MUST-authenticate-once-available with DaneFailurePolicy
[ ] Read sections 2.1 and 2.2 before designing the MX lookup
[ ] MX lookup DNSSEC-validated, with the status of both steps surfaced
[ ] Reference identifier set per section 3.2.2, matching per section 3.2.3
[ ] Placement decided and recorded"}
